# Methods before long reads

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## How this chapter's sources were read

Of this chapter's sources, many are pre-2000 and are held in this project's
corpus as abstracts rather than as full text, which bounds what can be claimed
from them. Every record behind the chapter was read against its cited lines by a
reviewer who had not written it, and the review changed 42 of them. Not one was
an arithmetic error. The corrections were hedges that had hardened, scopes that
had widened past the source, a reversed direction, and two fields that asserted
what their own claim denied.
:::

Every claim about alternative splicing has an assay behind it, and the assay
fixes what kind of claim it can be. A method that measures a length can
establish that a transcript is discontinuous without establishing that the
discontinuity is regulated. A method that counts junctions can establish
prevalence, and cannot establish which junctions occurred in the same molecule.

The sections below follow that constraint rather than the chronology, taking one
generation of method at a time with the specific thing it could not reach.

## Electron microscopy and a split transcript {#sec-1977}

Splicing was established by a physical measurement rather than by a sequence.
Berget, Moore and Sharp located adenovirus hexon mRNA on the viral genome by
examining RNA-DNA hybrids in the electron microscope [@berget1977spliced].

The inference rested on a length of unpaired RNA. About 160 nucleotides at the
mRNA's 5' end failed to pair with the single-stranded DNA encoding the rest of
the message [@berget1977spliced].

What the microscope could resolve had been stated a few years earlier by the
people who developed the staining. A single-stranded region appears about 8.5
nanometres thick against 3.5 for an RNA-DNA duplex, and a hybrid of about 80
nucleotide pairs can be recognised in favourable cases, with difficulty
[@wu1975gene32staining]. A later survey of the whole family of nucleic-acid
microscopy methods put their positional resolution at 50 to 100 nucleotides, and
presented the technique as the step that chooses which region to sequence next
rather than as a substitute for sequencing [@brack1981dnaem].

That resolution is visible in what the hexon paper reported. The three upstream
segments complementary to the unpaired tail were placed at 17, 20 and 27 genome
units, which is a fractional coordinate on a viral map rather than a nucleotide
position, and the paper closes by offering a model for late message synthesis
[@berget1977spliced].

A second group reached the same place by a different hybridisation geometry.
R-loops formed between viral DNA and unfractionated polysomal RNA resolved
three short segments from distant map positions, fused into one leader of 150
to 200 nucleotides [@chow1977amazing].

The R-loop had been published the year before as physical chemistry rather than
as a mapping tool. In 70 per cent formamide an RNA displaces the identical
strand of a DNA duplex, the structure forms fastest at the temperature where
half the duplex has separated, and it survives both removal of the formamide and
digestion with restriction enzymes [@thomas1976rloops]. A 1977 study of
adenovirus nuclear RNA sets out the whole inference chain the geometry
supported. Loop size is proportional to the length of the RNA that hybridises,
the molecules were measured in micrometres and ran as long as 13, and an SV40
sequence carried inside a hybrid viral DNA had to serve as a position marker to
orient the loops on the map [@meissner1977nuclearrna].

Two unlike physical assays put the same segments at the same coordinates.
Neither could give a sequence or an exact splice boundary, so the claim they
licensed was the narrow one that a transcript can be discontinuous.

What that claim displaced was the assumption that a message runs colinear with
the gene encoding it. A historian of the period records the dismissal of
universal colinearity as following from two things together, the substantiation
of the hybrid observation and a second group's parallel discoveries
[@fry2024anomaly]. The same account places the observation itself
inside a transcription-mapping project rather than in an experiment designed to
find it [@fry2024anomaly].

## Sequence fixed the boundaries and left an ambiguity {#sec-sequence-arbiter}

Hybridisation geometry bounded a region and sequencing named positions inside
it. At the adenovirus E4 locus the 5' termini were resolved to nucleotides 325,
326, 327 and 329, inside a region that microscopy and S1-nuclease gel mapping
had been able to map only as the message's 5' end [@hashimoto1981termini].

Sequencing also settled less than the sharp version of this story suggests. The
authors who sequenced the ovalbumin splice boundaries state that nucleotide
sequence alone cannot define unique excision-ligation points, because the
boundaries carry directly repeated sequence, and they reach unique points by
proposing them [@breathnach1978boundaries]. An independent survey of the same gene's
junctions found short homology at every one and no strong pairing between
adjacent junctions [@catterall1978junctions].

So the two generations of assay divide the labour rather than one replacing the
other. A retrospective records that cDNA sequencing later fixed most adenovirus
splice sites at nucleotide level [@westergrenjakobsson2021adenovirus]. One feature of
that virus is still reported only from the microscope, a third E3
polyadenylation site, and the modern authors who mention it write that messages
"might correspond" to it [@westergrenjakobsson2021adenovirus].

## A reaction in a tube, and the fidelity it did not have {#sec-in-vitro}

Moving splicing out of the cell made its requirements statable. A cell-free
reaction removed the first intervening sequence from an adenovirus major late
precursor and joined the first leader to the second, and the requirements came
out as protein, magnesium ions and ATP [@hernandez1983cellfree]. The same system
made the activity separable, since a postnuclear fraction had no splicing
activity alone but stimulated the nuclear extract, and that stimulating activity
travelled with small ribonucleoprotein particles on two kinds of chromatography
[@hernandez1983cellfree].

Accuracy was checked by primer extension, which showed the product's sequence
across the junction matching reticulocyte beta-globin message
[@kole1982invitrosplicing]. Those authors also stated their system's limits
without hedging. The efficiency was low, the substrate spliced most efficiently
was one terminated upstream of the polyadenylation site, and the transcript
terminated downstream of that site was not spliced at all
[@kole1982invitrosplicing].

Efficiency improved and exposed a dependence. A HeLa nuclear extract removed the
first intervening sequence from up to 90 per cent of an input human beta-globin
precursor under optimal conditions, and splicing needed neither correct ends nor
a poly(A) tail nor a cap. Without a cap, though, only about 30 to 40 per cent of
the precursor was spliced accurately, with aberrantly cleaved RNAs alongside
[@krainer1984faithfully]. The system earned its place by reproducing a disease
pattern, since beta-thalassaemia mutations placed in that intron caused the same
abnormal splicing in the tube as in cells [@krainer1984faithfully].

The reaction's intermediate was identified by three physical anomalies at once
rather than by sequence. The excised intervening sequence migrated anomalously
on polyacrylamide gels, reverse transcription was blocked near its 3' end, and a
nuclease-resistant component mapped to the same site. Those authors then proposed
a branched adenosine, placing it within a fragment 28 to 37 nucleotides from the
3' end [@ruskin1984lariat]. The same two anomalies turned up in intact cells of
another organism, where four forms of an excised yeast actin intron were
recovered and two ran unusually slowly, one of those also carrying the block to
reverse transcription, with the branch at the third adenosine of the conserved
UACUAAC sequence [@domdey1984lariatinvivo].

Extracts also accepted substrates their own organism would not. A plant
precursor carrying both its introns was processed in a HeLa extract with both
introns removed in order and the exons faithfully ligated
[@hartmuth1986plantpremrna], and an independent group reached the same
conclusion with two further plant introns [@brown1986plantintrons]. The same
authors set their result beside an earlier observation of their own running the
other way, in which a human growth hormone precursor was not processed in plant
tissue in cells [@hartmuth1986plantpremrna]. The two experiments differ in more
than direction, since one is an extract and the other is tissue, so the pair
does not establish a one-way compatibility.

The sharper mismatch is about specificity. A yeast precursor was spliced
accurately in a HeLa extract, and the extract branched it significantly nearer
the 3' splice site than the conserved sequence yeast uses in cells and in its
own extracts [@ruskin1986branchpoints]. Mutants lacking that sequence, which
yeast rejects both in cells and in extract, were spliced accurately by the HeLa
system [@ruskin1986branchpoints]. Those authors read the pair as one basic
pathway differing in the specificity of its components. What it bounds is
narrower and more useful here: an extract scoring as accurate on a gel is not
thereby using the cell's chemistry.

## cDNA clones and a regulated choice {#sec-regulated}

Immunoglobulin was one route to the next claim. The membrane and secreted forms
of the mu heavy chain travel on two different mRNAs, one of 2.7 and one of 2.4
kilobases. That came from restriction mapping and sequencing of cDNA clones
taken from a tumour making both chains [@rogers1980twomrnas].

Calcitonin was the other, and its authors drew the general conclusion.
Alternative processing of calcitonin gene transcripts yields distinct mRNAs
with different tissue distributions. They proposed this as a strategy:
developmental regulation of RNA processing as a way of increasing the diversity
of neuroendocrine gene expression [@amara1982alternative].

The same group later made the methodological argument explicit. Cloning
together with processing analysis could reach a complex neurobiological system
with no prior structural or biological information about the product it would
find [@rosenfeld1983production]. The method had become a way of discovering
biology rather than confirming it.

Establishing that a choice was regulated took a different kind of experiment
again, and the troponin T gene supplied two of them. Cloning and genomic
sequencing at the rat skeletal gene gave a minimum of ten and potentially 64
distinct messages from small exons with a split-codon structure, and those
authors name the observation that forces a regulatory explanation: at least two
of the messages are spliced from structurally identical primary transcripts, so
nothing in the substrate can account for the difference
[@breitbart1985combinatorial]. Moving the exons settled where the difference
sits. A construct carrying the gene's combinatorial exons was transfected into
muscle and non-muscle cells, and the alternative exons were incorporated as in
the native gene only in differentiated myotubes
[@breitbart1987transfactors].

Mutation pointed at the sequence doing the work. A series of mutant calcitonin
transcription units in HeLa and F9 cells showed cis-active elements near the
calcitonin-specific 3' splice junction to be the primary regulators of the
choice [@emeson1989spliceacceptor]. Hybridisation at the same locus had already
placed the calcitonin and pseudo-calcitonin sequences on one chromosome and
inside the same nuclear transcripts, with both messages functional and encoding
different polypeptides, which those authors offer as compatible with their
proposed model rather than as a demonstration of it
[@rosenfeld1982polymorphism].

The vocabulary arrived alongside. The phrase "alternate splicing pathways" is in
use by 1981 for a choice of route at the growth hormone gene, with the products
present in normal pituitaries [@denoto1981growthhormone], and "alternative
splicing" appears the same year in a microscopy proceedings account for families
of messages sharing their 5' and 3' ends [@broker1981visualization]. Those are
the earliest uses located here, under searches of abstract text, so an earlier
use inside a paper's body would not have surfaced. By 1987 a paper could open on
a definition rather than an introduction, calling the process ubiquitous and
describing single genes encoding multiple protein isoforms
[@breitbart1987transfactors]. Two years later the asymmetry was stated plainly,
with a good deal of information accumulating about constitutive splicing and
very little known about alternative RNA processing in complex transcription
units [@emeson1989spliceacceptor].

## RT-PCR and one locus at a time {#sec-low-throughput}

For roughly two decades after that, measuring splicing meant one locus and one
gene. RT-PCR was the conventional approach, and retrospectives written three
decades later still name it as such [@park2018expanding].

What the earlier assays physically produced is worth stating, because it bounds
what they could say. The RNA blot was published as a transfer technique in which
separated RNA is coupled to treated paper and specific bands are found by
hybridisation and autoradiography, so the output is a band at a position on a
gel [@alwine1977rnablot]. A systematic comparison of blotting procedures opens by
saying that detecting very rare messages this way is not straightforward, and
reports a floor of about 5 picograms of a specific sequence after days of
exposure with highly labelled probes [@gal1983blotsurvey].

Nuclease digestion of hybrids, read on a gel, did more. The year after the hexon
result it mapped the early messages of adenovirus 2, identifying seven abundant
cytoplasmic RNAs, every one spliced [@berk1978earlymrnas]. The same assay
produced the structural statement this chapter needs, that several messages from
one transcriptional unit share extensive sequence and differ in how genomic
sequences are spliced together [@berk1978earlymrnas]. At the growth hormone gene
S1 mapping found that one of four intervening sequences has two different 3'
splice sites [@denoto1981growthhormone], and in quail muscle S1 protection with
primer extension showed the 5' and 3' exon choices to be coordinated across
physiologically different muscles [@bucher1989troponint].

Solution hybridisation with nuclease protection was the more quantitative
alternative to RNA blot analysis. Its own practitioners recorded the catch,
which was that at a locus making several mRNAs by alternative splicing the
protected-fragment pattern from a uniformly labelled cRNA probe became hard to
interpret [@nucleaseprotection1989solution].

An assay can be sensitive without being diagnostic. In the S1 nuclease
configuration best suited to demonstrating a splice, unspliced and spliced RNA
both protect the probe across the junction. The assay was reported as not
diagnostic, and needed an RNase H pre-digestion to become one
[@sisodia1987s1artefact].

Quantifying a ratio by PCR has its own failure modes, and the people building
the assays named them. Reading product amounts off a reaction in its plateau
phase can be misinterpreted, tube-to-tube variation makes semiquantitative
results hard to reproduce, and levels measured with different primer pairs
cannot be compared, which is why target and competitor were co-amplified in one
tube with a single primer pair [@borson1998competitive]. Practitioners building a
real-time readout for splice variants opened by saying that getting an accurate
number out of the older assays had been laborious and limited in principle
[@vandenbroucke2001splicevariants]. One protocol adds a third primer pair in
sequence shared by both variants, because the variants differ in local secondary
structure and reverse transcription can run at different rates on them
[@camacholondono2016reliable].

How far the measurement misses has been quantified on defined inputs. With two
plasmids mixed at five known ratios, the two variant-specific shares should sum
to 100 per cent, and they fell short or over by at most 7 per cent and on
average 2.7 when amplification efficiency came from one estimator, against at
most 11.5 and a mean of 9.0 from another [@camacholondono2016reliable]. What
that measures is closure on 100 per cent rather than recovery of the input
ratio, and all three estimators ran on the same five mixtures, so the deviation
belongs to the efficiency estimate. The same authors state the assay's boundary:
it measures one splicing decision, not several in the same primary transcript,
and it returns a within-sample ratio rather than an abundance comparable across
samples [@camacholondono2016reliable].

The enzyme can also manufacture a variant. One group tested the assay rather
than the biology and re-attributed its own finding, after a reported deletion in
a colon cancer message reappeared from in vitro transcribed RNA, failed to
appear with two other polymerases, and removed 1,851 base pairs between two
direct repeats beside a stem loop [@mader2001templateswitching]. Scanning a
collection of human splice sites for the same signature put the artefact at a
significant share of apparent splices using non-canonical signals, while leaving
it rare across the collection as a whole, with the risk concentrated where a
putative intron is flanked by direct repeats [@cocquet2006templateswitching].

Protein-level confirmation was its own project. An isoform-selective antibody
could place a variant in a tissue, as it did for a muscle and heart form of
neuronal nitric oxide synthase whose purified enzyme was active
[@silvagno1996nnosmu]. Exon-specific antisera could go further and put a share
on it, showing one thyroid peroxidase form below 10 per cent of the protein
[@gardas1997tpoisoforms]. What a gel band could not establish is visible in the
same work, where a doublet differing by about 5 kilodaltons turned out to carry
the same exon-encoded peptide in both bands, and the authors read the size
difference as suggesting post-translational modification rather than the splice
[@gardas1997tpoisoforms]. Sometimes the protein was simply not there: an
antibody raised against the product predicted by a VDAC3 mRNA variant failed to
find it [@decker2000vdac3]. And the method with the best claim to separating
forms had a floor, since two-dimensional gels staining to low picomoles could
not visualise the separated amyloid precursor isoforms at all
[@newton2006appisoforms].

## Which junctions were in the same molecule {#sec-combinatorial}

The deeper limitation of the whole single-locus era was combinatorial, and it
outlasted it. As late as 2010, authors building a single-molecule splicing
readout opened by stating it plainly: studying linked regulation of multiple
splice sites within one gene, in transcripts such as Dscam, required new
approaches [@conze2010singlemolecule]. The arithmetic in @sec-dscam is precisely
what a bulk assay cannot report. Inclusion frequencies measured one exon at a
time are compatible with combinations across molecules that contradict each
other.

The arithmetic at an ordinary human gene is already large. Nine alternatively
spliced segments in CACNA1G define 512 possible transcript structures, and those
authors note that most have never been observed [@emerick2007correlations].
Reading whole molecules changed the answer there. A survey of 1,580 full-length
cDNAs from fetal and adult human brain found 30 distinct transcripts across 15
sites of variation, and the splicing shifted from nearly independent in the
fetal population to strongly concerted in the adult [@emerick2006cav31].
Measuring all 36 pairs of the nine loci, linkage rose with development for most
pairs, and the departure from independence was not confined to pairs, with the
adult population showing raised higher-order correlations for groups of up to at
least six loci [@emerick2007correlations].

Those authors also state what their measurement was for. The developmental
change is visible only once full-length transcripts are seen whole, and would be
largely invisible to a gene-expression measurement or to an array-based or
EST-based splicing survey [@emerick2007correlations]. Whether linkage is the
general case is a separate question, and the methods section of that same paper
raises the possibility that one or two pairwise interactions may account for the
departure from independence at some loci [@emerick2007correlations]. That is a
modelling remark rather than a result, and the Dscam work in @sec-dscam is where
independent choice has actually been measured.

Molecules were read whole before they could be counted one at a time. Long
reverse transcription, gene-specific second-strand synthesis, long PCR and
cloning produced full-length libraries for 21 ion channel transcripts, with the
exon combination of each clone read by multiplex PCR, about 85 per cent of
clones carrying a full-length insert, and variants as rare as one in a thousand
detected in linear proportion to their starting abundance
[@regan2000fulllength]. Counting replaced cloning next. Digital polony exon
profiling was presented as a way to watch, transcript by transcript, which exons
are included and in what combinations [@zhu2003singlemolecule]. Calibrated
against a defined input, that readout picked out a single alternative molecule
against upwards of 5,000 wild-type ones; separately, counting stayed linear over
a wide concentration range at an r-squared of 0.99
[@zhou2011cmybsinglemolecule].

Put side by side with a bulk assay at one locus, the two disagree by an amount
that has been measured. Across 13 paediatric leukaemia samples, with up to 3,000
molecules queried each, exon-level QPCR and single-molecule counting of c-myb
agreed closely on total transcripts at an r-squared of 0.946, modestly on one
variant at 0.815, and poorly on another at 0.244, with agreement for that
variant restored above 0.88 once the counted molecules carrying its junction
were pooled to imitate what the QPCR reports
[@zhou2011cmybsinglemolecule]. The reason is that an exon is shared by many
molecules. The single-molecule count found 21 distinct variants containing one
exon, of which one is predicted to make the corresponding protein, and 22
containing another, of which two do [@zhou2011cmybsinglemolecule]. Those authors
state the limitation in their own words: a QPCR assay reports one exon or one
junction per measurement, and cannot say which of several changes occurred in
the same molecule [@zhou2011cmybsinglemolecule].

By 2010 the problem had been posed as a distributional one. The authors of a
single-molecule assay note an apparent correlation between the choices made at
separate sites, as against those sites combining at random according to their
separate frequencies, and say that understanding it needs an assay returning the
splice patterns of thousands of full-length transcripts
[@conze2010singlemolecule]. Their own design states its ceiling with a number
attached, since four fluorescence channels and a combinatorial decoding scheme
would let ten serial hybridisations read as many as nine exons across as many as
324 genes [@conze2010singlemolecule]. The cost per locus was comparable. A
full-length cloning survey of one gene family needed thousands of molecules read
one clone at a time [@regan2000fulllength]. No source read here states how many
assays a genome-wide survey at that resolution would have taken, and multiplying
these figures is arithmetic this book is doing rather than a published estimate.

## A minigene reports on the minigene {#sec-minigene}

Transfecting a construct put the splicing decision under the experimenter's
control, and it moved the decision into a different piece of DNA. The scale of
that literature was counted once: a curation of every minigene described in
print held 82 entries carrying 97 ascribed regulatory sequences between them
[@stamm2005asd].

How far a construct and its own gene can disagree has been measured. A reporter
for Dlg4 exon 18 in mouse N2a cells included the exon in 27 per cent of its
mRNA, against a published endogenous figure of 66 per cent, and those authors
offer the different promoter, regulatory elements left out of the construct, or
decay of the skipped form as possible reasons [@zheng2013screening]. The 66 per
cent carries no cell type in that paper, and the same work notes that the exon
is largely skipped outside neurons, so the two figures are not a measurement in
one cell type.

The same authors state the general limitation and an artefact of their own
backbone. Minigenes do not always reproduce endogenous regulation, and flanking
sequence in the vector can confer responsiveness to factors that leave the real
exon alone [@zheng2013screening]. Their screen supplies the concrete case: a
factor that came out of the reporter screen was depleted successfully and
produced no change in the endogenous exon [@zheng2013screening]. Reporter
variability in that system was suspected to come from where and in how many
copies the construct had integrated, rather than from trans-factor levels, with
a correlation near zero [@zheng2013screening].

The construct's promoter decides part of the readout. Swapping promoters on one
reporter changed which splice site was chosen, including whether the exon
responded to two named factors [@cramer1999coupling]. Vector sequence can do the
same at the junction, where a cryptic site in the backbone was used in place of
the intended one [@rodriguezmunoz2022functionalassays]. A protocol written for
the assay states the honest claim plainly, that the absolute ratio is not the
result and the mutation-induced change is [@teng2025minigeneprotocol]. And a
negative in a construct is not a negative about the gene, as one group found when
their construct's truncated introns bounded the result
[@juan2014bimcis].

What the assay does deliver is a denominator. One panel of 15 variants returned
seven aberrant, which is a measurement of the variants rather than of the gene
[@rodriguezmunoz2022functionalassays].

## ESTs and the first genome-scale numbers {#sec-est-era}

Expressed sequence tags made a genome-scale count possible, and the counts did
not settle. The generating process is worth stating first, because its artefacts
become splice variants.

An EST was a read off one end of a cloned cDNA, with the sequencing reaction
starting in the vector and running into either the 5' or the 3' end of the
insert [@liu2006estbias]. Normalisation and subtraction, the two procedures that
made rare transcripts findable, work by letting denatured cDNA re-anneal so that
abundant species pair up and are removed, which destroys the relationship
between how often a sequence appears and how abundant it was in the tissue
[@liu2006estbias]. Across more than 900 mouse libraries, the combined steps of
reverse transcription and of choosing which clones to sequence can introduce
systematic bias into which transcripts a library samples, and the bias was
present even in libraries that had been neither normalised nor subtracted
[@liu2006estbias]. Those authors name the consequence: comparing dissimilar
libraries without correcting for the biases will likely produce statistically
significant and biologically meaningless differences, a source of error they
call significant and until then under-appreciated [@liu2006estbias].

The error classes were measured. Against a curated reference set, one collection
carried reversed clones at about 5 per cent and internal priming at about 2.5,
with lane-tracking errors near 0.5 per cent [@aaronson1996estquality]. Chimeric
clones, where two unrelated cDNAs share a vector so that one clone reports two
loci, came in at no more than one in thirty by mapping both ends of 30 sampled
clones [@seki1997chimericclones]. Reading raw trace files rather than cleaned
database entries exposed the wet-lab steps behind the rest, including failures
of the restriction enzymes, two inserts in one vector, concatenated adapters,
and 3' structures inside reads labelled as 5' ends [@zhou2012cdnaartifacts].

One of those artefacts was followed all the way to a variant count. Aligning the
whole EST set to the genome identified 53 heavily contaminated libraries holding
24,766 ESTs that probably represented genomic DNA, pre-mRNA or reads spanning
non-canonical introns, and those sequences would have produced 9,575 spurious
splice variants and 6,370 spurious genes in the clustering tool those authors
used [@sorek2003estlibraries]. That is a counterfactual about one pipeline rather
than an audit of a published catalogue, which is what makes it usable.

Against that background the prevalence series reads differently. Spliced
alignment of EST contigs in 1999 put alternative splicing at 35 per cent of
known human genes, with most of the detected variation in 5' untranslated
regions [@mironov1999frequent]. A different comparison a year later gave 38 per
cent, over 7,867 non-redundant mRNAs of which 3,011 carried an alternative form
[@brett2000estcomparison]. Mapping roughly 2.1 million mRNA and EST sequences
onto the draft genome raised it again, to 42 per cent or more
[@modrek2001genomewide]. Then the dependence was demonstrated rather than
suspected. With sufficient coverage nearly every gene examined showed some
alternative form, and requiring a variant above five per cent with statistical
support collapsed the yield to 17 to 28 per cent of 6,400 RefSeq genes
[@kan2002selecting]. By 2004 the counter-argument was in print, with cassette
exons seen only in EST databases differing systematically from cross-species
conserved ones and a significant portion argued to be aberrant splicing
[@sorek2004howprevalent]. @fig-prevalence shows what that does to a decade of
published estimates.

Getting an EST across a junction was itself an algorithm with assumptions. One
widely used aligner works in stages, which can miss small internal exons on its
first pass, and moves gap boundaries onto canonical sites where feasible
[@kent2002alignmenttool]. Another scores splice-site strength jointly with
sequence identity rather than treating the two separately
[@usuka2000optimalcdna], and practitioners of a third state the identity
assumption their predecessors had needed [@brendel2004consensusalignment]. The
group that runs GenBank named the failure modes: loci with paralogues,
polymorphic sites, sequencing errors, splice signals departing from the
consensus, and small exons [@kapustin2008splign].

A six-program comparison put a number on one of those. Judging each program's
EST alignments against its own alignment of the corresponding reference mRNA
over 218,641 human sequences, false terminal exons arising from mis-aligned
poly(A), meaning 3' exons at least 75 per cent adenine joined by a non-consensus
intron, affected 15.5 per cent of all mRNA sequences and 22.1 per cent of the
RefSeq subset under the worst program, against 2.12 and 2.72 per cent for the
next worst and 0.01 and 0.00 for the best [@kapustin2008splign]. That is a spread
of about three orders of magnitude between programs on identical input, and
those authors describe the segments as ones they suspect are poly(A) tails
rather than demonstrating it.

The splice-site assumption underneath all of it was quantified. Of 22,489
verified mammalian splice-site pairs, 98.71 per cent were GT-AG and 0.56 per
cent GC-AG [@burset2001mammaliansplicesites]. Of 171 non-canonical pairs with
EST support, 156 matched the genome, and those resolved into sequencing or
annotation errors correcting to the canonical form, genuine GC-AG pairs, AT-AC
pairs and three further categories [@burset2001mammaliansplicesites]. Resolution
is also limited by how close two real sites sit, and more than half of human
donor sites have another donor within three to six nucleotides
[@ermakova2007humangenome].

Clustering turned reads into genes, and the step changed the answer. Of
1,313,103 human ESTs, one build condensed 64 per cent into 143,885 tissue-level
clusters, while linking those clusters through clone identifiers gave 68,701
assemblies holding 81 per cent of the input [@miller1999clusteringapproach]. Two
projects did not produce the same genes, since one consolidated 1.86 times as
many ESTs as the corresponding build of the other, though neither source states
whether the inputs were identical [@miller1999clusteringapproach]. One algorithm
had its error rate measured, under-clustering at most 0.4 per cent of the time
and over-clustering at most 0.8, while agreeing with another project's partition
on 83 to 90 per cent of cases and joining sequences 8 to 20 per cent more often
[@burke1999validatedmethod].

Once a gene became a splice graph the catalogue was bounded by the model. One
human splice-graph database enumerated more than 1.2 million putative transcript
sequences, found alternative-splicing evidence in about 65 per cent of the genes
it examined, and reported that for 5 per cent of cases more than 100 transcripts
might come from one gene [@leipzig2004splicinggallery]. Another made the support
threshold part of the model, scoring each path's reliability partly by the
minimum number of clones needed to reconstruct its exons
[@kim2005estclustering]. And a confound sat underneath the whole exercise, since
some transcripts seen at one locus differ by the allele they came from rather
than by splicing, which one analysis put at 21 per cent of alternatively spliced
genes with a conservative lower bound of 6 [@nembaware2004transcriptisoforms].

The threshold is where the published numbers actually differ, and the cleanest
demonstration is inside one release of one database. The release holding 89,078
human relationships across 11,717 clusters reported alternative splicing in 53
per cent of the 22,220 multi-exon genes it covered, and in 75 per cent, 10,202
of 13,690, once the gene set was restricted to genes with at least one mRNA
sequence [@kim2006asapii]. Those authors attach two properties to that
restriction, a gene model likely to be full length and generally higher EST
coverage, and the second figure is a subset of the first rather than the same
genes under a different support rule. Elsewhere the rule is explicit and
different: one study accepted a pair of competing sites only when each was
supported by a protein, a full-length mRNA, or ESTs from two or more independent
clone libraries [@ermakova2007humangenome], and another reports support per
transcript instead of a prevalence at all [@pospisil2004splicedatabase]. A
chicken EST survey states the practitioner's version, that breadth of tissue
sampling sets the answer [@tang2007alternatesplicing], and one published
catalogue reports its own sensitivity and specificity rather than a headline
fraction [@wong2008splicingpatterns].

Conservation was offered as the arbiter, and its yield was low. Combining mRNA
and EST evidence with whole-genome alignment found at least one event conserved
in both the human and mouse transcriptome at 1,964 of 19,156 loci, 10 per cent,
which those authors call a lower bound [@sugnet2003humanmouse]. The statistical
and conservation filters broadly agreed, since variants surviving the
five-per-cent selection were conserved in mouse ESTs and validated against
GenBank mRNAs at significantly higher rates than the rest [@kan2002selecting].

The filter's own chance pass rate was then measured. Taking random intronic
regions bounded by canonical dinucleotides as pseudoexons and running them
through the identical test, average conservation in rat usually fell between
0.05 and 0.15 and depended on length, so those authors calculate that of every
100 mouse candidate exons tested for rat conservation, 5 to 15 would pass by
chance [@nurtdinov2009rodentexons]. The same group argues that conservation
between two close species may not be sufficient to claim an exon is functional,
because chance activation of cryptic sites inside an already-conserved region
manufactures a conserved-looking exon, and because an exon missing from a sparse
outgroup EST collection cannot be inferred absent from its genome
[@nurtdinov2009rodentexons]. Both errors would over-estimate the number of
functional rodent-specific exons.

They also separate the two kinds of species-specific exon, and the direction
matters. Exons found only in mouse occur at the same frequency across every
group of genes, which those authors explain by most of them not being real,
while exons conserved in mouse and rat but absent from human and dog rise from
slowly to rapidly evolving genes and are commoner in duplicated genes
[@nurtdinov2009rodentexons]. After their own pseudoexon correction the estimated
number of real rodent-specific exons stays non-negligible in every group, which
they read as evidence of exon birth [@nurtdinov2009rodentexons]. So discarding
exons seen in one genome only removes little that is real, while demanding
conservation outside the rodent lineage removes the class carrying that
signature.

The databases that held all this were literature-curated before they were
computational. One was assembled from protein annotation, by analysing Swiss-Prot
entries and clustering proteins that could arise from one gene, and held about
1,700 sequences [@gelfand1999asdb]. A plant census meant searching GenBank and
PubMed for every reported gene and then merging and reviewing the hits, which
yielded 168 genes across 44 species [@zhou2003pasdb]. The curators of a later
resource name the mismatch they had to build around, that their literature and
computational sets differ in how far annotation goes and in the vocabularies
they use, so the interfaces absorb the heterogeneity rather than reconcile it
[@stamm2005asd]. That resource's computational half held events, introns, exons
and per-isoform peptide sequences, all generated from gene-transcript
alignments, beside a manually curated literature half
[@stamm2005asd]. Counting units differed too: one project's first release
reported 30,793 alternative splice relationships
[@lee2003annotationproject] and its next reported nearly 90,000 distinct events,
a threefold expansion, where the later paper uses both words for the same
quantity [@kim2006asapii].

## Arrays and the designed survey {#sec-arrays}

Arrays moved the measurement from discovery to a designed survey, and the design
step is where the method's character sits. Splicing-sensitive arrays did not
begin with alternative splicing at all. One of the earliest was built in budding
yeast to tell spliced from unspliced RNA at each intron-containing gene, and it
was used to read the genome-wide consequences of losing each of 18 mRNA
processing factors, with gene-specific indexes absorbing the changes in
transcription and decay those losses brought [@clark2002splicingspecific]. Its
calls were checked against a one-locus assay rather than taken alone, and
quantitative PCR confirmed what the array had indicated about introns whose
branchpoint sits close to the 3' splice site [@clark2002splicingspecific]. A
later group describing that design calls it a printed two-colour array carrying
oligonucleotides against exon, intron and junction regions, reporting a
splice-junction index and an intron-accumulation index, each being the relevant
probe signal divided by the gene-level signal
[@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. Carrying the approach to vertebrate alternative
splicing made the design annotation-dependent by construction, since the
oligonucleotides are chosen from gene models that already encode which
alternatives exist [@srinivasan2005splicingsensitive].

The surveys that followed were large and fixed in advance. Junction microarrays
carried a probe for each junction between adjacent exons across more than 10,000
multi-exon human genes, measured over 52 tissues and cell lines, and their
authors concluded that at least 74 per cent of such genes are alternatively
spliced [@johnson2003genomewide]. Combining exon-body probes with junction
probes on one platform made tissue-specific splicing quantitative for thousands
of exons in mouse [@pan2004revealing]. One human compendium designed arrays
monitoring 203,672 exons and 178,351 junctions across 17,939 genes
[@castle2008differential].

What a fixed probe set costs is visible in what went into one. A prototype human
exon array was built by projecting four gene-prediction programs together with
RefSeq and GenBank mRNAs and dbEST sequences onto the November 2002 assembly,
parsing the union into probe selection regions of median length 119 base pairs,
and the design as built held 1.4 million such regions and upwards of 9.6 million
unique probes [@clark2007tissuespecific]. Its designers left junction probes off
on purpose, reasoning that a junction design can only enumerate junctions
already observed and that the fullest list then available remained substantially
incomplete [@clark2007tissuespecific]. The next generation put eight probes on
each probeset and covered 315,137 exons and 260,488 junctions, a set chosen to
cover the events for which mRNA or EST evidence already existed
[@shen2009madsplus].

The blind spot the chapter inherited needs restating against the designers' own
account. A 2008 RNA-seq survey noted that alternative 5' and 3' splice sites
shift the message by a region often too small to interrogate with a probe
[@wang2008alternative]. The array's designers had addressed exactly that,
splitting overlapping exons with different edges into separate probe regions so
that shifts in site usage could be seen, and they state the limit: no region
shorter than 17 nucleotides could be given a probe, so splice sites shifted by
less than 17 nucleotides were left out of the design
[@clark2007tissuespecific]. That line is a statement of design intent. Nothing in
that paper demonstrates the detection, since its own validation focused on
cassette exons, so the claim that arrays could not see shifted splice sites is
unsupported rather than refuted.

Underneath every splicing call sat a measurement whose physics differs from
gene-level measurement. On exon arrays a probeset stands for one exon or part of
one and is generally four oligonucleotides that often overlap substantially,
and the closer spacing made it harder to select probes of similar GC content, so
melting temperatures vary more and neighbouring probes' signals are less
independent [@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. Probe affinity is written into the
standard model as a per-probe term, and the model's authors name bad probes,
false annotation and alternative splicing itself as the routine sources of
outliers that robust estimation exists to absorb [@laajala2009probelevel]. A
gene-level index therefore has to be computed from a selected subset of a gene's
probes, because some are saturated by background, some cross-hybridise and some
fall in alternatively spliced regions [@xing2006probeselection]. Even background
subtraction is a modelling choice with a measurable cost, and replacing a
GC-matching default with a sequence model raised the variation explained in
background response from 0.07, 0.24 and 0.25 to 0.24, 0.30 and 0.35 in three
tissues [@kapur2007exonarrays].

Cross-hybridisation was measured rather than assumed. In a dilution series
replacing labelled mouse RNA stepwise with labelled Drosophila RNA, the
all-Drosophila condition identified fewer than 4 per cent of probes as
cross-hybridising, and those were removed [@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. Probe
response is also partly predictable from sequence, and a positional dinucleotide
model found CG-rich probes to under-respond and AT-rich probes to over-respond
[@gaidatzis2009overestimation].

The metric that carried the era is a difference of logarithms. For one probeset
the splicing index is its log expression change between two samples minus the
gene's log expression change, which decouples exon inclusion from transcription
only under two assumptions, that a change in a gene's expression moves most of
its exons and that alternative splicing happens less often than constitutive
inclusion [@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. As implemented on one junction array,
the index is a single probe's background-corrected intensity divided by the
gene's estimated expression index, and an event is called when two one-sided
tests per probe, summarised by Fisher's method, put the skip probeset and at
least one include probeset below a cutoff with opposite directions of change
[@shen2009madsplus].

The first assumption was then shown not to hold. The relationship between a
gene's expression change and the spread of its exons' splicing indices appears
on real exon-array data, and those authors propose an arithmetic reason rather
than a biological one: probe response curves differ and are nonlinear, so as a
gene's expression rises its probes' signals drift apart, and a gene-level
estimate pools enough probes for that to average out while an exon level built
from four sometimes-overlapping probes does not
[@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. They report alternative splicing events
overestimated 12-fold, with that figure applying to genes differentially
expressed between the samples compared rather than to genes in general
[@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. A cross-platform test separated artefact from
biology, since the same analysis on deep sequencing of three mouse tissues showed
none of the relationship [@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. The artefact also
reproduces across species because probe sequence is conserved, with homologous
response slopes correlating at 0.426 measured and 0.588 predicted, so a
cross-species comparison can report conserved events where none exist
[@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. Those same authors state the limit of their own
explanation: predicted and observed slopes correlate at 0.528 in mouse and 0.468
in human, weakly enough that they cannot exclude some biological contribution
[@gaidatzis2009overestimation].

The alternatives each changed one assumption and kept the rest. One tests
whether all interaction terms of a two-way analysis of variance are zero,
another scales the index by within-group variance, a third rebuilds the
gene-level estimate from only a gene's least variant exons, and a fourth models
an exon's expected behaviour against a robust gene estimate and calls splicing
where the fit is departed from [@gaidatzis2009overestimation]. That fourth
replaced the ratio with an outlier test, scoring an exon by the median residual
of its probes divided by their median absolute deviation, a formulation built
for experiments without replication [@laajala2009probelevel]. Its own authors
report assessing it on simulated data, a panel of 11 human tissues and 10
matched colon pairs, with output including exons confirmed by RT-PCR but no
confirmed fraction given [@purdom2008firma]. A statistician's account names what
each method rests on, with the index and the analysis-of-variance test both
depending on probe intensity rising linearly with concentration, and a
generative alternative limited by design to two isoforms
[@gelfond2011rankchange]. Which test the platform's manufacturer stood behind is
reported two ways in the literature, and the two accounts should not be read as
agreeing [@gaidatzis2009overestimation; @laajala2009probelevel].

Simulation put a number on what the linearity assumption costs. Over 1,000
simulations with no true differential splicing, the analysis-of-variance test
gave false-positive rates of 0.063 and 0.057 under linear response and 0.165 and
0.194 once a logistic response spanning the array's dynamic range was imposed,
against 0.000 to 0.010 for a rank-based alternative
[@gelfond2011rankchange]. The same confounding then appeared on real data from a
different platform, where the evidence that test reported rose with a gene's
estimated fold change while the rank-based method's did not
[@gelfond2011rankchange].

Head to head, the methods separate mainly by how many exons of a gene are
spliced. At a noise level those authors take as typical, with one differentially
spliced exon per gene all eight procedures scored 0.94 to 0.99 area under the
curve, and with five the probe-level method held at 0.92 or above while the
others fell to 0.79 to 0.88 [@laajala2009probelevel]. Ranked against
RT-PCR-confirmed exons in a colon-cancer dataset, the best-ranking confirmed
exon came 4th, 5th, 26th, 28th, 35th, 50th and 82nd depending on the method,
while the probe-level procedure placed two confirmed exons in its top ten
[@laajala2009probelevel]. In both of those comparisons the winning method is the
evaluating authors' own, which is worth saying because it is not true of every
comparison in this literature.

Validation rates bound the whole era, and the two that exist are not
comparable. On a prototype exon array, 27 of the 32 brain-enriched probesets
with the most significant index values showed clear enrichment by RT-PCR, 84.4
per cent, 21 of the top 23 ranked by magnitude did so, and 72 of 84 predicted
tissue-enriched probesets were confirmed across the project, 86 per cent
[@clark2007tissuespecific]. That rate is bounded by what was eligible: only
internal events with constitutive flanking exons were tried, nothing at the
edges of transcript clusters, and no probeset mapping to an annotated alternative
polyadenylation region, terminal exon or start site
[@clark2007tissuespecific]. The larger figure is the weaker one. A junction-array
analysis reports 88.5 per cent, 153 of 173 events tested, cites it as
unpublished data, and states no criterion for calling an event validated
[@shen2009madsplus].

Underneath every splicing call sat a present-or-absent call with its own error
rate. Scoring exon probesets as present and intron probesets as absent across 71
constitutively expressed housekeeping genes gave a median sensitivity of 0.88
and a median specificity of 0.82 at one cutoff [@clark2007tissuespecific]. And a
good deal was discarded before any index was read, including about 6.8 per cent
of probesets for mapping to more than one location, leaving 10,148 probesets with
significant brain-against-non-brain differences of which 2,161 in 1,097 genes
were brain-enriched [@clark2007tissuespecific].

The headline number from the designed era needs its definition attached. Of
19,221 transcript clusters entered, 12,139 were detected in at least two of 16
tissues, and 8,837 of those had at least one probeset passing the index test in
at least one of 120 pairwise comparisons, which is 72.8 per cent
[@clark2007tissuespecific]. Those authors state what their design could not
count: because the index registers only a change between samples compared, a
gene expressing several isoforms in the same proportions everywhere returns
nothing, so the figure counts genes with tissue-variable exon usage rather than
genes with more than one isoform [@clark2007tissuespecific].

What the designed survey could establish that EST data could not was the
existence of exons absent from the sequence databases. Of 2,161 brain-enriched
probesets, 287 were supported only by gene-prediction algorithms and by no cDNA
sequence at all, several were verified in brain transcripts by cloning and
sequencing, and the analysis reported 17 novel exons in 11 genes together with
six previously unseen arrangements of annotated exons
[@clark2007tissuespecific]. A designed probe set can only ask about what was
designed in, and that is the one thing it could ask that a sequence database
could not.

## RNA-seq and the near-universal estimate {#sec-rnaseq-arrives}

RNA-seq removed the design step, and the 2008 mouse reference datasets rested on
41 to 52 million mapped 25-base reads from poly(A)-selected RNA of three
tissues. They yielded a junction census of about 145,000 distinct splices, with
roughly 3,500 genes expressing one or more alternate internal splice
[@mortazavi2008mapping].

A parallel human study reported 94,241 splice junctions from two cell lines, of
which only 4,096 were previously unidentified. Exon skipping was the most
prevalent form of alternative splicing [@sultan2008globalview]. The companion
study behind the near-universality claim sequenced 12 to 29 million 32-base
cDNA fragments per sample, from ten human tissues and five mammary epithelial
or breast cancer cell lines [@wang2008alternative].

The most-quoted figure needs its provenance attached, because the claim that
about 95 per cent of multi-exon human genes are alternatively spliced is not a
pure RNA-seq result. Its source states that the estimate came from combining
mRNA-Seq with EST and cDNA sequence data [@pan2008deepsurveying].

The companion number is an extrapolation over a stated denominator. Multi-exon
genes, 94 per cent of all RefSeq genes, were binned by read coverage and a
sigmoid was fitted. The asymptote lands near 98 to 100 per cent of multi-exon
genes [@wang2008alternative].

The same paper carries a more conservative figure bounded by a threshold.
Requiring a minor isoform to exceed 15 per cent of the gene's output in at least
one sample gives 92 per cent of multi-exon genes. Those authors rescale that to
about 86 per cent of all human genes [@wang2008alternative].

![Ten years of estimates of how many human genes are alternatively spliced. The
denominators differ, the abundance thresholds differ, and two of the values are
extrapolations rather than counts. The spread is the subject, and reading the
column as a rising trend reads nine questions as
one.](../figures/prevalence-estimates.svg){#fig-prevalence width=100%}

What that figure counts, and under which conditions, is taken up in
@sec-how-functional.

The instrument also stopped being one thing. Which junctions a short-read
library supports depends on how the RNA was enriched before sequencing. In blood
libraries sequenced both ways to about 50 million paired reads, the ratio of
junction read support between ribosomal-depleted and poly(A)-selected libraries
rose with transcription length [@natrajgayathri2026polya]. Coverage along a
transcript is not uniform either, and the non-uniformity is set by the same
step, with ribosomal-depleted libraries showing a lower coefficient of variation
than poly(A)-selected ones for transcripts above 5 kilobases
[@natrajgayathri2026polya]. On four muscle biopsies split between the two
protocols, the poly(A)-selected libraries missed many of the novel and cryptic
events in one long gene that the depleted libraries of the same patients
reported [@natrajgayathri2026polya]. Measured directly on reconstruction
accuracy, the same in vitro transcribed RNA gave different accuracy under the
two routes, with poly(A) selection worse across every algorithm tested
[@hayer2015benchmark].

Three more preparation choices leave signatures in the data. Random-hexamer
priming leaves a nucleotide-composition bias over the first 13 positions of a
read, reproducible across organisms and laboratories, and the authors who
identified it stated that non-uniform read placement directly degrades the
comparison of an alternatively spliced exon against a constitutive one
[@hansen2010biases]. Fragmentation leaves a reproducible footprint rather than
random breakpoints, with the variance in where reads start on spike-in
transcripts predicting it in other samples of the same protocol at mean
r-squared 0.77 and 0.85 [@parekh2016impact]. And most reads that look like PCR
duplicates are not, since computationally identified single-end duplicates ran
from 36 to 74 per cent of reads, were explained largely by sampling and
fragmentation bias, and removing them raised the false discovery rate by about
two percentage points in two datasets [@parekh2016impact].

Strand information is a fourth, and it is what an unstranded library does not
have. Measured as leakage onto the wrong strand, the four best protocols in one
compendium put 0.47 to 0.63 per cent of reads antisense to known transcripts,
and those authors name resolving overlapping transcripts and the boundaries of
adjacent genes on opposite strands as what strand information buys
[@levin2010comprehensive].

## Short reads could not reconstruct a molecule {#sec-short-read-limit}

The full-length reconstruction problem was named in the EST era. The
high-throughput methods of the day returned detailed information about short
fragments only. Recovering whole isoform structures from a fragment mixture was
posed as a separate inference task [@xing2004multiassembly].

Short reads inherited that problem, and the Cufflinks authors state the
limitation in their own opening paragraph: assembly and abundance estimation are
hard because a read generally cannot be attributed to one isoform
[@trapnell2010transcript]. They also record what they had done instead in
earlier work, which was to quantify genes without allocating reads among
alternative isoforms, while still reporting evidence that several forms were
co-expressed [@trapnell2010transcript].

Before any of that, a read has to be placed. A community assessment of spliced
alignment ran 26 protocols from nine development teams, with two further
versions added by the assessors themselves, over 76-nucleotide paired-end data
from a human cell line, mouse brain and two simulated transcriptomes
[@engstrom2013systematic]. On identical input, yield ranged from 68.4 to 95.1 per
cent of read pairs, mean 91.5 with a standard deviation of 5.4
[@engstrom2013systematic]. A program that truncates a read end rather than
failing on it places more of the library, at the cost of placing it partially,
and the program that does not truncate had a lower yield for that reason
[@engstrom2013systematic].

Right locus is not right boundary. Between 96.3 and 98.4 per cent of spliced
reads were placed at the correct location, while every base was correct for only
60.3 to 89.3 per cent [@engstrom2013systematic]. Accuracy improves when the
splice sits away from a read's ends, and most protocols lose sensitivity below
about five supporting reads, so a junction count is a thresholded quantity rather
than an observation [@engstrom2013systematic]. Novel junctions are also largely
method-specific, with 52 to 54 per cent of one program pair's novel junctions
absent from every other mapper [@engstrom2013systematic]. Annotation changes the
picture in both directions, recovering nearly all expressed known junctions
while also placing reads at thousands of annotated junctions that most protocols
reported where the simulated transcriptome never expressed them
[@engstrom2013systematic]. Linking more than two exons inside one read was
recovered at 79.3 per cent with annotation and 72.1 per cent as the best
annotation-free figure, and two programs never reported more than one splice at
all [@engstrom2013systematic].

Reads also disperse. Every protocol placed primary alignments across more genes
than had produced the reads, with 80 million reads originating in 16,554 genes
and alignments landing across upwards of 17,800, an excess the assessors
attribute largely to pseudogenes [@engstrom2013systematic]. The assessors' own
list of what remained unsolved names multi-mapped read placement and false exon
junctions [@engstrom2013systematic].

Multi-mapping has been quantified from several directions. In the 2008 32-base
human library about 60 per cent of reads were unique to the genome and 4 per cent
unique to junctions, so by those authors' own arithmetic about two thirds could
be assigned unambiguously to individual genes [@wang2008alternative]. On perfect
100-base pairs from 19,654 genes, 4.33 and 2.97 per cent were non-unique under
two aligners, with 843 genes under-counted and 586 assigned zero
[@robert2015errors]. The affected genes are families and pseudogenes, and on real
mouse data 27.8 to 43.9 per cent of reads could not be assigned
[@robert2015errors]. Read length does not fix the hardest part, since across
21,459 paralogous human genes three read lengths gave equal numbers of reads
mapped to those genes, which those authors report as a surprise
[@chhangawala2015impact]. Equal totals are consistent with equally wrong
placement, so what that measures is read count rather than correct assignment.
Read length does change the junction catalogue, where only 8 to 9 per cent of
known and 1 to 2 per cent of novel junctions were found at all four lengths
tested [@chhangawala2015impact].

Assembly is where the reads become models, and the step is not determinate. The
assembler's own description says so: fragment alignments become nodes in an
overlap graph, the graph is decomposed into the fewest chains explaining the
reads, and because that minimum decomposition is not guaranteed unique it
chooses among equally parsimonious assemblies by weighting edges with a
percent-spliced-in value [@trapnell2010transcript]. An independent benchmark
locates the false positives in that step, since local evidence is assembled into
global transcripts in every way consistent with the short reads, and intron
signal present at some level almost everywhere becomes long exons
[@hayer2015benchmark].

Measured against known structures, the error rate is substantial. On in vitro
transcribed RNA from 1,062 human cDNAs where 95 per cent of transcripts had only
one form, every algorithm tested predicted false transcripts numbering at least
20 per cent of the true ones, and missed at least about a quarter of the true
ones [@hayer2015benchmark]. Accuracy does not improve with coverage in the
expected direction either, and on a realistic simulation stratified into
coverage bins precision often fell as coverage rose
[@hayer2015benchmark]. Depth does not rescue the human case, where transcript
detection stayed low despite exonic coverage above 4,000 read pairs per
kilobase, and at least one consistent isoform was recovered for more than half
of highly expressed genes in fly and worm against only more than 35 per cent in
human [@steijger2013assessment].

The community assessment of reconstruction found best-method transcript-level
recovery falling as the genome got more complex, at 56 to 59 per cent of spliced
protein-coding transcripts in *C. elegans*, 43 per cent in *D. melanogaster* and
21 per cent in *H. sapiens* [@steijger2013assessment]. Those figures were scored
under a relaxed rule, because transcript ends were effectively unrecoverable
from 76-nucleotide paired-end data, so predicted first and terminal exons were
allowed to differ from the annotation at their outer edges and a transcript
counted as recovered when its splice sites matched with both ends free
[@steijger2013assessment]. The same assessment separated the two failure modes
and found both active. For most transcripts not every constituent exon was
detected, and even where all exons were reported the methods frequently could not
link them into a complete isoform [@steijger2013assessment].

Read length buys assignment, and the amount is measurable. Comparing two
Illumina paired-end libraries from the same cell line, 25.04 per cent of
assignable 75-base reads matched exactly one annotated isoform, against 32.98
per cent at 262 bases [@cho2014highresolution].

How large the wall was is best seen in what two pipelines do to identical input.
Ten differential-splicing tools run on the same data called between 0 and 4,506
genes on one cohort and between 11 and 14,313 on another, and the best
between-tool overlap of top-ranked gene lists was 35 and 45 per cent
[@mehmood2019systematic]. A separate comparison asked a different question,
matching events by coordinate and comparing the inclusion values of events both
tools had called, and found exon skipping agreeing above 0.8 while retained
intron fell below 0.5 [@muller2021computational]. Those two results are not in
conflict, because ranked gene lists and the values of jointly called events are
different comparisons, and the one thing both agree on is that retained intron
is where everything falls apart. Structure agreement does not give abundance
agreement either, with correlations against an orthogonal platform running from
0.34 to 0.68 across methods [@steijger2013assessment].

An incomplete model set produces a wrong answer rather than a missing one. The
Cufflinks authors report that restricting their analysis to known isoforms would
have given an incorrect abundance for a known isoform of one gene and would have
missed the novel start site that dominates before differentiation
[@trapnell2010transcript]. And of roughly 105,000 catalogued events of eight
types, reads supporting both alternative forms were observed for more than a
third in the library behind the near-universality estimate
[@wang2008alternative], which leaves fewer than two thirds and is a statement
about what was observed rather than about what was resolvable.

Depth does not substitute for length, since reads that map to several places
stay common however deeply a library is sequenced, so more data does not remove
that uncertainty [@zheng2022nonidentifiability]. The limitation is formal as well
as practical. Different sets of transcript abundances can generate the observed
reads with equal likelihood, so the maximum-likelihood answer is not unique, and
the underlying true expression cannot be determined from the reads
[@zheng2022nonidentifiability].

The field's response was to stop asking for full-length structures. Event-based
tools count reads over particular exons and junctions and report a
percent-spliced-in value, measuring one decision instead of solving for the
whole molecule [@park2018expanding]. One model-based estimate of isoform ratios
reported with a statement of confidence appeared in 2010, which is where the
field moved from a designed ratio to an inferred one [@katz2010miso]. That is
where PSI comes from, and @sec-psi gives what it costs.

Thirty years of method development had converged on a measurement that
answers a smaller question very well. The smaller question leaves out the
molecule, and getting it back took a longer read, which is @sec-one-molecule.
